_note: A1 — the LOGIN-TRIGGER fold (completeness/A1-auth-hardening.md H2). LoginHelper decides, on EVERY main-frame navigation, whether the URL about to load is a configured identity provider; a match cancels the app's own navigation and hands the URL to a spoofed-user-agent web view that shares the app's cookie jar. A raw `hasPrefix` therefore hands an attacker who controls `idp.example.attacker.invalid` a login surface wearing the IdP's clothes. The rule pinned here: a configured prefix that PARSES AS AN ABSOLUTE URL is pinned to its exact scheme, host and port and refuses userinfo; a configured prefix that is not a URL keeps the legacy raw-prefix behaviour, because deployments configure bare host fragments and silently dropping them would disable their logins. Both halves are load-bearing and both are cased below. isAllowedAuthorizationUrl is the second half of the same policy: what LoginHelper's Android launcher will hand to a browser at all.

matchesConfiguredTrigger._note: matchesConfiguredTrigger(candidate, configuredPrefix). The raw prefix is a NECESSARY condition, never a sufficient one: it is checked first (so nothing that fails the legacy test starts matching), then an absolute prefix additionally pins the origin. Case is deliberately NOT folded on the prefix test — an uppercase host that fails the byte prefix simply does not match, which is the fail-closed direction (the navigation proceeds into the app surface it was already going to).

isAllowedAuthorizationUrl._note: isAllowedAuthorizationUrl(raw) — what the Android launcher may hand to a browser. Confidential transport only, a real host, and no URL credentials: a javascript:/intent:/file: authorization start is never an authorization start, and userinfo in an authorization URL is a phishing primitive that some browsers still render.
